utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can I invite you to shine some light on the way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was hoping that you would shine some light for me. I don't know best how to proceed. I do know that I've tried to make some inquiries regarding what would happen if the 98 bis motion were stayed for a while and we got some kind of positive decision or positive feedback from the US about General Clark, how soon he could physically be here if other hurdles were eliminated. I don't have a firm answer for that, Your Honour. It could be -- from the information I have, it appears it wouldn't be a matter of days, it would be more a matter of weeks or maybe even into May in terms of availability. I think I should let you know that, because that may have an impact on how you choose to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has there been discussion among counsel to see if --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So you're no further forward than you were yesterday. You believe that you can close your case, have the 98 bis hearing, and then apply to re-open it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if I could succeed in that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, but that's on the argument of -- I think the wording in fact of the principle might be evidence not available to you at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Depends on the definition of "availability," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in the past, it's really been a question of whether the evidence existed or was known about. This is a rather different -- I'm not suggesting --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not saying it doesn't fall within that idea. I at the moment don't know. But -- we seem to be on the same wave --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- length as to what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly doesn't fall in the traditional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- way that it's been interpreted but I see an argument that we can a make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And you're going to take -- your position is you're prepared to take a chance on the success of that argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, because of the history in connection with this particular matter, I just don't feel that I'm on firm ground to ask you to wait for a while for some indefinite possibility that may or may not happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- when we've all worked so hard and have had a strong interest in getting this case completed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't feel hidebound by technical issues such as the fact that there is an order that your case should close on the 23rd of March. You're in a different situation from the one you were in when you said you would close it on the 23rd of March, slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I hope it's not that that's stopping you and that you're looking at a much broader picture and the reality rather than the technicality of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. It's -- it's a reluctance, Your Honour, to put us all on hold for some sort of uncertain future. If I knew for sure that we succeeded that everything -- all obstacles would be removed and that General Clark could come here and testify within a reasonably short time-frame, then I would say, Yes, Judge, I'm requesting that let's delay the 98 bis until that can happen. But because I don't feel firm about when that might be, that's my hesitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, our position is subject to what you just said that you ordered this case to close the 23rd of this month. We're prepared to proceed to 98 bis submissions Monday morning and that's where we stand. The Prosecution could have called its witnesses any time since the case opened in July; that's an important factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only if we allowed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, they were on notice of May, Your Honour, of last year about these Rule 70s and Rule 70s are complicated by their very nature and one could ask why would you wait until the last week of a trial when you know that you have a high-ranking US general with all the circumstances that surround Rule 70, but we'll leave it with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, but what we would at all costs want to avoid is creating complications that we don't require. So it would be very easy for us just to say, Well, we'll postpone the 98 bis and make sure it takes place after all the Prosecution evidence has been led rather than get into deep water over technical issues. I mean, it is attractive to do it next week, but there are attractions about not doing that. I think we will require to adjourn to consider this. Before we do, there's a couple of things I think I can deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A motion was presented on behalf of Mr. Lukic for judicial notice of facts affecting the evidence of the witness Protic, a very succinct and, if we may say so, precise statement of the clear legal basis for refusing this application is set out in Mr. Hannis's response. I'm taking this one home to frame it, Mr. Hannis. And in the circumstances, since the motion doesn't satisfy either branch of the test under Rule 94, we deny the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, we can probably save you and Mr. Hannis and the planet the use of unnecessary paper for filing by regarding the joint Defence and Prosecution submission for admission of P924, 936, 930, 934, and 937 as made orally and dealt with orally. So we grant admission to these documents. You don't need to do anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just one last matter. Yesterday I informed you that we had agreed with the Prosecution on certain documents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you asked me whether the stipulations were by all accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: They all agreed. I have the document in my hand which just needs signing. I think it's probably more efficient to actually file this because there's a long list, but it's agreed by all parties and it just needs to be signed this morning and filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you give me a copy of that just now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This one I think is best dealt with the way you suggest, Mr. O'Sullivan. I'm interested, though, in other connections with the widespread reference to Vojska. These are all examples of publication in Serbo-Croat and then English translation following on that, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct, CLSS translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I can return that to you to deal with through the filing process. I want to ask you another question. Applications have been made for provisional release. There's an issue over the appropriate stage of dealing with the applications, assuming time runs and they're responded to in the usual way. If we postpone consideration of the 98 bis motion - if, I say, we postpone it - do you accept that it wouldn't be appropriate to deal with these applications until we had dealt with 98 bis? Or do you want us to consider them in advance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think you'll see that the obvious timing of these motions is that it would be the close of the Prosecution's case. I don't think the postponement of 98 bis would affect that situation. I think that if Your Honours want to allow the Prosecution the normal time-frame to respond, that's fine; if you want to expedite it, we have no objection to that either. I think the matter can be dealt with in the normal course. I don't see a connection between the 98 bis and our application. The connection we saw was the close of the case or the close of the evidence, so I think it can be dealt with forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- [Interpretation] Submission that was precisely linked to a 98 bis. I thought that I was supposed to write it afterwards and that's why I didn't submit it so far. So you'll probably receive the same submissions from other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The beginning of this intervention was not heard because the microphone was not activated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have copies of three. Well, the Chamber will adjourn and consider the question of when it's appropriate to hear the 98 bis submissions, and we'll resume as soon as we've decided what to do. Let's set 10.00 as the time, and if it's later, a message will be conveyed to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, this is the simplest question I think I could possibly ask you: Do you rest your case now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I guess with the provision that -- I should tell you there's one additional matter I need to bring to your attention concerning General Vasiljevic. You'll recall in his testimony about a Joint Command meeting on June the 1st. He indicated that he had an entry in his diary which he did not have with him. We have since received that entry. It's being translated and I do want to submit that when it's translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I make it clear that resting your case will be subject to the disposal of any currently pending matters, which will be resolved by tomorrow, and if it's a translation issue of that nature we, would permit you to file the untranslated document marked for identification and allow you to have it taken into account in the 98 bis submission as long as you were able to present to us at least a draft in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, and I'm sorry to appear to be vacillating at this point, but during the break I thought about everything that was discussed earlier. We would like to be able to present General Byrnes to you -- I mean, Mr. Byrnes and General Clark to you and Mr. Lilic, but we haven't been able to do that. If we had a recess of 30 days I don't know if we would be able to get some or all of them in. I would like to do that. That's my hesitation in saying: Yes, I rest now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we take it your position is now different from yesterday and indeed from this morning earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, having considered all the remarks that were made and thinking -- trying to weigh the pros and cons, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's the effect of the expiry of a recess of 30 days combined with a successful appeal and the non-availability of any other witness by that date, including General Clark?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then, if I understand your question, at that time if we are not able to produce any of those individuals, then we would rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, your comments on this new situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly a new situation. I go back to the order you made that the Prosecution would close. I see that you're maybe inclined to be re-considering that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I was anxious -- we're all anxious to be sure that this wasn't seen as something imposed by the Trial Chamber. That order was simply a reflection of what the Prosecution said they would do on more than one occasion. We weren't in an adversarial situation making a determination that there would be a completion of the Prosecution case by then; on the other hand, when we left the bench a short while ago we did think the simple answer to the question I had just asked would be yes, but it's not. So before we decide what to do, you have an opportunity to address us.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, this is a very important matter and there are six of us on this side, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we're off again. The -- one other thing that's developed here, though, is a time-frame that's at least manageable, whereas earlier this morning we were faced with an uncertain time-scale with an indication of a possibility of being in the month of May before we heard the evidence, never mind proceeded to 98 bis. So at least this is a firmer indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we think it appropriate to give you some time to consider your position. How long do you wish?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, 20 minutes, 30 minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's make it quarter to 11.00. The reason for asking that question was that whatever way the matter was decided on the strength of the earlier position taken by Mr. Hannis, it's possible to see legal issues further down the line. And I hope you'll excuse us for trying to foresee what is going to be the simplest way forward in the long run. That's what we had been trying to work out. We are very sympathetic to the idea of closing the case today and having the 98 bis hearing. And we can see certain legal issues down the line if we do that, but equally if we don't hear it immediately, we can see perhaps fewer legal issues but other practical issues down the line. And we are trying to simplify the future for the Trial Chamber and for the parties as best we can. So we'll give you the time you ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just perhaps you can clarify this for us before we go back and discuss it. What is unclear, to me at least, is the timing of the appeal against the Clark ruling. There's no -- I don't think there's any indication or any way of knowing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I've actually had an indication, but I don't know if I can share that with you because it was very informal and I don't know how firm it is. I'm happy to make inquiry just now to see if something definite can be projected, and if I can, I'll have that information given to you. I was purely curious and got a very, very informal indication, which I couldn't rely on at this stage. We'll resume at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, our lives aren't long enough for us to ask Mr. Hannis again about this matter, so I'll go straight to Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour was quite right yesterday when you said the one saga in the trial had ended. We submit that you should put an end to this second saga. We oppose the request by the Prosecution, which we all have received in the last half-hour, to allow the case to remain open for the period of 30 days following an Appeals Chamber decision on the Clark certification and in that time to seek to call three witnesses, Clark, Byrnes, and Lilic. And here are the reasons why we oppose that. Yesterday, and I'm referring to page 12096 of the transcript, the Prosecutor was quite clear. He said that the Prosecution rested. He said on that same page that we could proceed with the 98 bis submissions on Monday. And when asked: "What happens if someone has been acquitted by then?" Meaning after the appeal. The answer was: "Well, that's the Prosecution's loss." The Prosecution was prepared to close its case. Now, before I turn to Clark let me address the submission that the Prosecution has made in relation to Byrnes and Lilic. There's absolutely no connection between the pending appeal on the Clark decision and Byrnes and Lilic. The Prosecution cannot use the serendipity of the Clark appeal to attempt to keep its case open to call other witnesses. In other words, if this Chamber had not certified the Clark decision, Byrnes and Lilic would be out, the case would be closed. Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute provide that the accused must receive a fair and expeditious trial. Byrnes and Clark are out -- Byrnes and Lilic are out. Thank you. Now -- that's it. In regards to General Clark we say that the Prosecution's position was made clear, that if an appeal succeeds they would move to re-open its case. Now, again we say that there are issues of fundamental fairness and due diligence on the one hand and issues regarding the timing of disclosure which is still pending, and I'll deal with both. Your Honour put the Prosecution on notice last May of -- in relation to every Rule 70 witness, telling the provider to make up its mind. And we've been in this courtroom now since July of last year, and if the Prosecution ran the risk of waiting until the 11th hour to bring a major Rule 70 witness, I say the Prosecution has to live with the consequences of having been told as early as May of last year that this could happen. Now, in relation to disclosure, I wish -- I think to assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't tell me anything, Mr. O'Sullivan. What are you saying are the consequences of that, bearing in mind that it's in the hands of the Appeals Chamber now?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The consequences of that are precisely what the Prosecution said yesterday: We proceed with 98 bis Monday. If the Chamber's decision is reversed, it applies to re-open and if someone's acquitted, that's his loss. I have in hard copy, which I think may assist the Chamber and the parties, and I could ask the usher to distribute a copy to the Bench and one to the Prosecution. And while that's being distributed, Your Honour, this is a filing made on behalf of General Ojdanic, and I'm going to speak in connection with the pending disclosure in relation to General Clark, should he be a witness. You have before you General Ojdanic's opposition to motion to call General Wesley Clark as a Prosecution witness and it's dated 28 December 2006. And I would direct you to page 9497, that's the stamp number at the top right-hand corner of the page, 9497. My submission here is that on the assumption that the Appeals Chamber reverses your decision and Wesley Clark can be called as a witness, there is still pending from the Rule 70 provider disclosure. And you'll see the letter that I've referred you to at 9497. It's from the US Embassy to General Ojdanic's counsel. And you can see that the US government has taken the position that it's premature under Rule 70 to provide materials to the Defence until and unless there's an order from the Chamber granting certain protective measures for the testimony of General Clark. Now, this raises a number of issues, we say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, let me read this. The page I'm looking at doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it should be -- it's page -- at the bottom it's page 12. It's a letter dated 12 December 2006 from the Embassy of the United States to Mr. Peter Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything about the Chamber granting protective measures, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it's the last sentence of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It says -- it begins: "I'm writing to inform you that the United States Government has conditionally authorised General Clark. The authorisation is contingent on the Prosecution securing a court order granting certain protective measures."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But they don't go on to say, do they, that dealing with the inquiries needs to be delayed?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. I believe the letter in the second paragraph uses the word "it's premature to disclose the materials as requested under Rule 70." In other words, the American position is that until there's an order from this Chamber granting the protection sought, there is no disclosure, and I can represent to you that the Ojdanic Defence has not received any disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But read the whole thing, Mr. O'Sullivan. "We believed these requests were premature. At the time it was not clear whether General Clark would be authorised to testify. Consequently, it was not evident which subject areas would fall within the scope of cross-examination. Now that we have conditionally authorised testimony on specific areas, we believe it would be appropriate to re-visit this issue."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I assume there's been ongoing communication for the last three months between the Ojdanic team and the American government.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I can perhaps leave it to Mr. Visnjic who is much more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And perhaps it might be appropriate for him to respond to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to the documentation that we have at our disposal here, we have had a certain correspondence with the US government. No material has been received from them. Moreover, not knowing about how things would turn out today we wrote and filed today a letter that should have been sent through the Registry, and I believe Mr. O'Sullivan has a copy on his desk and it would be a good idea if a copy of that document could be made available to you and the Prosecution so that you can see for yourselves at what stage of disclosure we are currently with the US government and with NATO. To date, we have not received a single document from them --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but it's come to my attention that these letters, because they're discussing Rule 70 matters, may actually be confidential matters and that shouldn't be part of the public proceedings at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not necessary for the detailed terms of these to be discussed at the moment. We've got the documents and can look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just give you some additional information. We had planned to file this letter today, thinking that a decision would be made today about 98 bis, and we wanted to remove from our shoulders a possible problem of undue delay on the part of the Defence. What I want to say, and Mr. O'Sullivan has already raised this issue, when and whether these documents are going to be disclosed may affect the testimony and the evidence by General Clark; and depending on that, we may take further legal action that may lead to further delay of Mr. Clark's evidence, even beyond what the Prosecutor has told us about. So that there is -- there are more problems than mentioned previously with that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what's been happening since the 12th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from 12th December until today, according to the information I have here, there has been a certain communication. They asked us to specify our request and include more details, but I don't have all that communication here. If you give me some time, I'll come up with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds like a matter which will have to be addressed as and when and if it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. I just wanted -- in fact, all of us wanted to emphasise the complexity of this issue and the consequences that setting a precise date for General Clark's testimony may cause. We believe that everything is too uncertain at this moment for us to be able to state our position any more precisely, which in its turn makes it incumbent upon us to decide to what extent this make effect an efficient and fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you something else to say, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. Just to sum up then: We say that we should proceed with 98 bis Monday. Let the Appeals Chamber deal with the Clark decision as it sees fit. The Prosecution can take its position thereafter, and we should -- the case should close and we proceed to 98 bis Monday. And just parenthetically, not to deviate at all from what I have been saying, is that keeping this case lingering as it is - and of course we would also say Byrnes and Lilic are out - but keeping this case lingering as it does may very well have an impact on the fairness of our preparation time during the Defence case. And we should not be punished, the Defence should not be punished for any lack of due diligence on the Prosecution's part for not calling its witnesses in a timely fashion and dealing with all the issues that would arise particularly in relation to a Rule 70. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not immediately obvious why preparations for Defence cannot continue in the interim.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, that's quite correct, but, Your Honour, the accused need to know when the Prosecution case closes against them. They need to know -- there has to be some closure and some certainty, and that's only fair. That's only fair to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't disagree with that, Your Honour, but if you grant our request, there will be certainty as to when that date will be. It will be no later than 30 days after the appellant decision on the pending matter regarding General Clark. And to the extent that we are successful in persuading you and actually being able to get General Clark and/or Mr. Byrnes and/or Mr. Lilic here to testify and if they actually do testify, I certainly think it would be fair to the Defence -- if it took three weeks for that to happen and it included a week of preparation time for cross-examination of those witnesses, it would not be unfair for Your Honours to give them an additional four weeks for preparation of their Defence case to make allowance for the additional work that they've had to do in connection with the Prosecution case, but I may be getting ahead of ourselves a bit here, but I did want to make that remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan has raised a legal issue in relation to the commitment to rest the case which we consider we have to give further thought to and we will adjourn to do that and resume at 1.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Chamber has determined that yesterday the Prosecution did not close its case. An indication to the effect that the Prosecution rested was given. That was then questioned by the Trial Chamber in light of the outstanding appeal filed in the course of yesterday. The Prosecution reconsidered their position, as invited by the Chamber, and now proposes that closure of the case should be stayed for 30 days -- until 30 days after the appeal is determined. What we have decided to do is this: We have decided that we will stay closure of the Prosecution case until at least the 16th of April, and in order to give effect to that, we will vacate that part of our order of the 5th of March which specified the 23rd as the deadline. On the 16th, if the appeal has failed and the Prosecution has available either Byrnes or Lilic, then we would expect these witnesses to be led then, there and then, and in their absence to proceed straight to hear the 98 bis submissions. If the appeal succeeds, we would expect to be told precisely when Wesley Clark would give evidence. We regard the Prosecution motion as a clear statement that they would not request that he give evidence so that they are at dates which would prevent closure of the Prosecution case within 30 days of the determination of the appeal. Beyond that - and I'm thinking of the possibility of Byrnes and Lilic or either of them being available at some stage - we would require to address that as a separate issue on the 16th of April if they were not available on that date to give evidence. I want now to deal very briefly with the remainder of orders that are required leading to the commencement of the Defence case. We do not see this as having a significant impact on -- or such a significant impact on preparation of the Defence case as to require alteration of the order we've already made in respect of the 65 ter lists. The lists have to be compiled and they can be modified, if necessary, in the light of evidence made, but the list will be the list and available for that purpose. That's how we see it at the moment, and we find it difficult to think that this will change it but I will hear submissions on that in a moment. In connection with that, we would also like to hear further that the Defence believe that being given a significant period of time between now and the start of the Defence case will result in a shortening of that case; in other words, that what's happened since that indication was previously given confirms that that indication was an accurate one. Mr. Ackerman, I think we would like to hear from you on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You want to hear from me on that now, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I don't misunderstand, Your Honour, you're saying has anything happened since you -- since we last had communication about that to indicate that our position that we can shorten up the Defence case by this use of time is a correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The indications you've been given so far are that the gap between the Prosecution and the Defence case or the substantial -- the bulk of the Prosecution -- the vast bulk of it and the commencement of the Defence case is far longer than has been given in any other case to date in the Tribunal. And we want to be sure before we finalise the arrangements for the commencement of the Defence case that you're confidence that this period will profitably result in a shortening of the Defence case has not been dented by anything that's occurred in the intervening period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is not, Your Honour. I think if -- at least I can only really speak mostly from the Pavkovic Defence standpoint, because I haven't been in touch with the other teams regarding their preparation to this point, but I can tell you that everything's that's happened since then in terms of our preparation along that line gives me solid reason to believe that we are going to winnow things down over time and shorten our Defence presentation as a result. I think it's pretty clear to me that that is going to happen. As long as I'm on my feet, with regard to the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It seems to me that the period of time that we spend back in this courtroom after the 16th of April, whatever that period of time is, is time we would have been meeting with witnesses and putting together our Rule 65 ter materials. So whatever amount of time is taken away from us by additional time in this courtroom is time we've lost in that process. And assuming that your June 15th date was reasonable - and I have no argument that it wasn't - then it's also reasonable to extend it by whatever amount of time is taken away from us by additional time in the court. Because those days after the 16th of April would have been spent working on 65 ter and not in here cross-examining witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if -- I wonder if we maybe misunderstand each other on that. There was a view which was not given effect to in that decision that there's really no reason why a 65 ter list shouldn't be available very shortly after the end of the Prosecution case. And the real issue is when you demand the start of the Defence case, because it's preparation that's involved, whereas the list should be capable of production and the real work you should be doing would be on preparing in light of that list, which can be cut down as you get to the stage or expanded, for that matter, as you get closer to the trial. So we eventually fixed a date that we were all comfortable with as giving -- having heard your submissions that you did want a later rather than an earlier date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's why we're not so impressed by the idea of altering that date but have yet to make a final decision on the date when the Defence case will commence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if there is -- if there is a great deal of flexibility with regard to alteration of the 65 ter list after the 15th, then I see no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- but there is -- you've seen what we've done with the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- we could hardly do less in relation to the Defence, and I see Mr. Hannis nodding his head indicative of a reasonable approach. So unless there's anything else, then I would propose to hear what Mr. Lukic has to say because he looks somewhat more exercised on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and basically you know that even from the beginning we disagreed with my learned friend Ackerman on the time-frame we need for our Defences. Obviously, it would be different time we need for our Defence than Mr. Ackerman needs for his Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was I wrong in thinking, though, that you were getting rather concerned about the idea that the 15th of June would remain the date for the 65 ter lists?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem we have is the lawyers from this team haven't spoken to our witnesses yet. We haven't -- we didn't have time to speak to a single witness. The truth is that our investigators did -- had contacts with our witnesses, but we haven't. So we have to go through -- because your instruction is that this 65 ter motion should be very precise, and we have to include the summaries of their statements. We don't have a single one -- and documents that should be introduced with those witnesses. So that's why I'm concerned. I can give you a bunch of documents and a bunch of witnesses, but we have to combine it and to give you the summaries of their statements, and we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to qualify the demands we made. We do expect that you'll do your best to achieve the results that we've invited you to produce, but you are going to be the last, I anticipate, to present a Defence case, albeit that also hasn't been finally decided. But I suspect that's the way it will work, and therefore you've got more time to give notice of changes that occur after the 15th of June than anyone else has.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then -- thank you, Your Honour, then we are fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Anyone else wish to speak on this subject? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I assume that what I will say now may be premature in relation to some dates Your Honours have already set, but I wish to draw attention to the following: Should the scenario occur where all three witnesses testify, not only would this shorten our time, as Mr. Ackerman said, for preparing our Defence because of the time spending in court, but also because of the time we have to spend preparing for those witnesses. And disclosure, as I'm reminded by Mr. Zecevic. Not only will we spend time in court but also we will spend time preparing to cross-examine those witnesses. What I wish to say now is that this will affect the time we have planned to talk to our witnesses, and in the nature of things it should lead not automatically but to a reasonable argument for our arguments to extend the deadlines. So this is not now a motion; it is just a general expression of concern. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other comment? Well, we'll just briefly confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we are prepared to do -- and there will be a written order dealing with this aspect of the case. We've actively considered this in light of what's been going on this morning, and we are prepared to move the judicial recess so that it is included in the time between now and the re-start of the trial -- or at least the start of the Defence case. The effect of that would be to delay the start of the Defence case until the 30th of July, but if we do that, then there will be Judges missing during the month of June -- sorry -- the month of July, which means that the date for the 65 ter lists really has to remain where it is. And we would propose then having a pre-trial conference a week after that, on the 22nd of June. Pre-trial conference doesn't need to involve more than one counsel from each accused, and it's a matter for counsel and their clients, but so far as the pre-trial conference is concerned, if you decide to nominate somebody to represent your interests, then we will have no real difficulty with that, but it would have to be somebody fully instructed and you may find that it is necessary for one from each party to attend. Now, we hope that that is a sufficient period to enable the case to get started, bearing in mind that, apart from Mr. O'Sullivan, you will all have a bit longer than that. Of course, he might surprise us, and more than he will need to be ready, but if he does present a Defence case then that's going to give more time to everyone else to prepare theirs. It will be soon enough at the pre-Defence conference to debate opening statements and other issues of that nature and the order in which you will present your cases, if there's any question of that being other than the order of the indictment, and any other issues. Indeed, you'll be asked to contribute to an agenda before we have that meeting. Now, are there any matters arising from that that anyone wishes to raise at this stage? Well, these details will be confirmed in a written order, and that will be issued no later than tomorrow. We shall now adjourn until the 16th - is that at 9.00 or is there a court available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall need to notify the time to you, because there is at the moment on the schedule another case at 9.00 that day, but hopefully we will be here at 9.00 on the 16th; failing that, some other time on the 16th either here or in another courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of April, 2007

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.31 p.m.,
